title: Post‑mortem: observed outcomes in Experiment 005 after adding the “Preserve Editorial Intent” clause
description: A focused post‑mortem that reports what this single controlled experiment observed when the Narrative prompt gained one new generic section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” It will: summarize the experimental design (three baseline runs reused, three candidate runs with only the Narrative.user.prompt change, same commit and OpenAI / gpt‑5‑mini); present the measured differences (Narrative mean 6.00 → 4.00; Compose mean 5.67 → 3.33); identify consistent candidate failure modes (criterion C — orchestration became central; criterion D — unsupported additions such as validation intent and new audience framing); and record the operational decision (do not promote; rollback to the byte‑for‑byte baseline as recorded in the report, SHA‑256 475A9DB1CA028EBC927C99ECDD3DAB061B0616ED06FB1278879992D2E8DD795A). The piece will explicitly frame findings as observations from this experiment (correlation, not proof of causality) and list the experiment’s stated limitations (three runs per condition, no seed/temperature control, possible model‑alias backend changes, Synthesis outside scope). Governance implications will be presented as testable hypotheses tied to observed failure modes (for each suggested guardrail, state which failure it addresses and the minimal experimental prerequisites required to validate it: isolate the variable, increase sample size, set seed/temperature if available, include Synthesis‑level controls). The post‑mortem will close with concrete next‑step experiment proposals (each as a hypothesis with prereqs) rather than prescriptive policy.
audience: Nuëyon prompt engineers, product managers, and model‑governance reviewers who must evaluate prompt changes before promotion and plan follow‑up tests
rationale: Technical reviewers need an evidence‑accurate account that avoids overclaiming causality while giving enough operational detail to reproduce, audit, and design targeted follow‑ups. Framing governance implications as hypotheses with required test prerequisites keeps recommendations actionable but not prescriptive, matching the report’s limitations and decision context.
evidence: Source report (2026‑11‑04): candidate added a generic “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” section; controlled comparison used three baseline runs (reused) and three candidate runs with only Narrative.user.prompt changed, provider OpenAI / gpt‑5‑mini. Scoring tables show candidate mean totals fell (Narrative mean 6.00 → 4.00; Compose mean 5.67 → 3.33). All three candidate Narrative and Compose runs failed criterion C (orchestration became central) and criterion D (unsupported additions introduced: validation intent/commitment, audience of founders/product leaders). Decision: “Do not promote” and production prompt restored byte‑for‑byte (baseline SHA‑256 475A9DB1CA028EBC927C99ECDD3DAB061B0616ED06FB1278879992D2E8DD795A). Reported limitations: no seed/temperature control, small sample (three runs per condition), possible backend variation behind model alias, and Synthesis stage outside experiment scope.

title: One‑page leadership memo: Experiment 005 outcome and evidence‑bound next steps
description: A concise executive memo summarizing the experiment question, the single prompt change, the controlled comparison and headline metrics, the main observed failure modes, the promotion decision, and conservative next steps framed as testable hypotheses (e.g., ‘Hypothesis: adding an explicit audience‑restriction check will reduce unsupported audience additions; prerequisites: isolate the change, 10+ runs, fixed seed/temperature if available’). The memo will include the essential caveats so nontechnical approvers understand the evidentiary limits and why the change was rejected.
audience: Senior leadership, release approvers, and product managers who need a short, actionable summary with explicit caveats
rationale: Leaders need a short brief that records the operational decision and its empirical basis while avoiding policy overreach; presenting follow‑ups as hypotheses preserves rigor and prevents premature governance changes.
evidence: Report shows candidate prompt added a generic editorial‑intent clause; scoring tables and analysis list consistent failures on editorial hierarchy (C) and factual restraint (D); final decision: “Do not promote” and restored production prompt SHA‑256 475A9DB1CA028EBC927C99ECDD3DAB061B0616ED06FB1278879992D2E8DD795A. Limitations noted: three runs per condition, no seed/temperature control, possible model‑alias backend changes.

title: Pre‑promotion checklist for editorial‑hierarchy prompt changes (derived from Experiment 005)
description: A practical checklist mapping the experiment’s rubric A–E to review steps prompt reviewers must perform before approving edits that affect editorial hierarchy. It will require: publishing the exact prompt diff; running a minimal pilot with more runs than the experiment (recommend 10+); isolating variables (only one prompt file changed per pilot); documenting outputs and hashes; scoring outputs against A–E with an explicit hard gate that disallows unsupported factual additions (criterion D). The checklist will include mitigation for the report’s limitations (use fixed seed/temperature when available; note model‑alias backend risk; include Synthesis‑level inputs when appropriate).
audience: Prompt authors, reviewers, and CI/CD gatekeepers validating prompt edits before promotion
rationale: Experiment 005 exposed recurring failure modes and a usable rubric; converting those into a conservative checklist helps teams fail fast and collect sufficient evidence before promotion decisions are made.
evidence: Report provides a 0–2 scoring rubric for A–E and flags criterion D as a hard promotion gate. Artifacts and diffs are indexed (prompt‑changes/Narrative.user.prompt.diff; candidate/prompts/Narrative/; baseline/ and candidate/ outputs). Reported limitations (small sample, no seed) inform checklist requirements for stronger validation prerequisites.

title: Reproducibility playbook: how to rerun Experiment 005 and extend it safely
description: A technical playbook with exact steps to reproduce the experiment and conservative extensions to improve rigor: checkout commit, build commands, run the console, swap in variant prompts, capture Narrative and Compose outputs, and compute rubric scores. Extensions will recommend increasing run count, freezing seed/temperature if possible, and systematically isolating prompt changes (e.g., only audience wording or only the editorial‑intent clause). The playbook will list required artifacts to record (diffs, outputs, logs, SHA‑256 hashes) so auditors can compare outcomes to the reported observations.
audience: Engineers and auditors who must reproduce the experiment, validate the decision, or run follow‑ups with stronger statistical rigor
rationale: The report gives exact operational details; packaging them into a reproducibility playbook plus safe‑extension guidance reduces ambiguity and supports rigorous audits and subsequent experiments that can move from correlation toward stronger causal inference.
evidence: Report includes checkout path and commit (main, be882989a7b7956e1b57199f143e7cf434fbe4e5), run and build commands (dotnet build; dotnet Nueyon.Compose.Host.Console.dll), model/provider (OpenAI / gpt‑5‑mini), artifact locations (baseline/, candidate/, prompt‑changes/), and recorded hashes for baseline and restored production prompt SHA‑256 475A9DB1CA028EBC927C99ECDD3DAB061B0616ED06FB1278879992D2E8DD795A. Reported limitations (no seed/temperature, three runs) motivate the recommended extensions.
